articles.title: WordPress Releases Canonical MCP Adapter Plugin via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
WordPress has officially released a canonical MCP Adapter plugin that also maintains backward compatibility. Now users who want to add AI functionality to their site can choose the official WordPress MCP Adapter plugin.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard developed by Anthropic that lets AI systems securely connect to apps, data, plugins, tools, and websites, enabling AI to access information and perform actions. For WordPress websites, MCP enables AI to interact with sites, plugins, and WordPress functions (PHP code snippets that perform specific tasks like publishing posts).

Jason Adams, Director of Engineering, AI at Automattic tweeted :

“The WordPress MCP Adapter is now released: https://wordpress.org/plugins/mcp-adapter 🎉

This is the canonical MCP plugin for WordPress, carefully architected for backwards-compatibility with MCP versions. If you want MCP in your site or plugins, I highly recommend using this.

…It makes use of the Abilities API to avoid functional redundancy while handling authorization. I’m excited to see the pieces coming together!”

“The backwards compatibility matters. WordPress plugins tend to stay around for years.”

“Agreed, and we can’t control the backwards-compatibility of the MCP protocol itself, so making a way for this in our ecosystem is important.”

The MCP Adapter plugin has been around for some time but it was previously only available through the official WordPress MCP Adapter GitHub releases page , which is why it already has over 40,000 installations. Version 0.70 is the first version to be published in the official WordPress.org repository.

Review the details and download the official WordPress MCP Adapter plugin here or install it through your WordPress admin dashboard.

articles.title: ADWEEK Commerce Advantage: Amazon’s AI-Driven Future Leaves Some Buyers Weary of Losing Control
articles.fullContent:
By Lauren Johnson ADWEEK Advantage is part of a series where every month, our top editors interpret what happened in each vertical, and what it means for the future.

At Amazon’s annual UnBoxed advertising event, the retail giant outlined an overhaul of its core ad platform to integrate chat-based features and AI.

Dubbed Amazon Ads Agent, the platform aims to integrate AI into all advertiser workflows, including two campaign types—DVA+ and full-funnel campaigns—that recommend which formats advertisers should buy to hit goals, from upper-funnel streaming campaigns to lower-funnel search ads.

While advertisers can apply controls, Amazon is pitching the revamped ads platform more broadly as a way for Amazon’s AI to guide advertisers’ spend and strategies.

“Amazon Ads Agent helps you move faster and with more confidence,” Kelly MacLean, vp of Amazon Ads, said during the keynote session at UnBoxed. “When you’re spending less time on mechanics, you get to ask the better question: What else is possible for my brand?”

Amazon Rebuilds Its Ad Platform Around AI Agents In the short term: advertisers flag transparency issues

Despite the rise in AI, some advertisers are wary of having agents control ad buys, specifically when it comes to execution and optimization, said Zach Ricchiuti, vp of strategy at Kepler.

“When it comes to actually making decisions, that’s where we still have people stepping in and making decisions,” he said. “That’s the nuance that you still need.”

That said, Ricchiuti said there are use cases for agents to automate planning, research, and building campaigns.

He also warned that Amazon’s tools could be another example of a black box , similar to Google’s Performance Max, where advertisers lose some audience transparency and control for performance. In the case of Amazon’s tools, the company said that its AI can recommend which formats advertisers should buy based on a campaign’s budget and goal.

“It took a lot of years for Performance Max to be a product that people trusted,” Ricchiuti said. “The job of a brand and agency is to be skeptical of what a black-box solution is—there should be a healthy dose of skepticism around, like, what media and what audiences are actually being bought.”

In the long term: advertisers are using more agentic tools

At the same time that ad buyers are skeptical of black boxes, more agencies are using agentic-based workflows and tools.

In the past year, Amazon-focused adtech firm Gigi has pivoted its business from helping brands buy streaming ads to managing agencies’ spend and operations with Amazon’s demand-side platform.

Adam Epstein, cofounder and CEO of Gigi, said that marketers are still looking for custom, bespoke agents that help agencies with individual ways of working, especially with Amazon’s trove of properties and data.

“We have the concept of a holistic view of the customer,” he said.

In other cases, agencies have their own agentic tools for managing Amazon.

Omnicom Media Group, for example, has its own tool, similar to Amazon’s, that recommends where clients should spend money within Amazon. Omnicom also owns data firm Acxiom, which can track ad impressions to sales, said Mike Feldman, global head of commerce at Omnicom Media Group.

“Every product we build is agentic-enabled with MCPs [Model Context Protocol servers],” Feldman said, referring to the open standard that lets AI agents connect to and operate software tools.

Lauren Johnson is Adweek's deputy editor of commerce, where she runs Adweek's retail and influencer marketing coverage. Before joining Adweek in 2024, she was an advertising reporter at Business Insider for six years and previously covered technology for Adweek.

articles.title: Why Advertising Will Be Key to Shaping Our AI-Powered Future
articles.fullContent:
By Joe Marchese Today’s headlines are dominated by AI, and rightfully so. Are machines the new gods or the greatest bubble in history? Either way, this wave of AI will define a course for humanity.

But for all the talk about AI, we’ve spent far too little time talking about the business model that led us here: advertising. This is the story told in my new book, Human Dot AI .

If “advertising” sounds too boring, think of it instead as the business of shaping human opinion at global scale—the attention economy. Advertising is the business model that underlies many of the largest tech companies in the world and shapes the information diet of billions of people.

But all of this only matters in the context of what comes next in a world with generative AI. How will news and entertainment change? What skills will we all need when we can talk to machines, and they can talk back to us?

Advertising has an important role to play in the generational technology shift that is upon us, and those of us in the business have a responsibility to make sure advertising doesn’t misalign AI with human interests.

How our current media diet, and the world we know, was shaped by machines (early AI) seeking advertising.

How being good at being human, and connecting with other humans, has always mattered most and will only matter more in the age of AI.

What comes next in a world of generative AI and how the business model of advertising (the fight for our attention) will shape human lives as well as the future of the most important technology ever created.

I’m sharing an excerpt from the introduction of Human Dot AI below to illustrate how different—and in some ways, very familiar—the attention economy looked when I was just starting out in the advertising business.

Human Dot AI will be published Nov. 10 by Amplify Publishing Group. Preorder your copy here .

2019, Tokyo, 5 a.m. I was pacing around the pool of the Park Hyatt, the hotel immortalized in Lost in Translation, the film in which Bill Murray plays a world-weary actor summoned to Japan to film a Suntory whiskey commercial. With the neon lights of the city blinking forty-seven floors beneath me, incredibly loopy from the jet lag, I was suspended in time. And for the second time in my life, I was fired by a mouse.

I’d been expecting the call from Disney HR. It had been on the calendar for months. I’d always loved climbing—trees, mountains, buildings (if my Tokyo setting was any indication), and jobs. And now I was going to fall, or at least take the express elevator down.

I was leading an organization that was responsible for multiple billions of dollars in advertising for sports, broadcast, and cable television at Fox Networks Group, one of the world’s most powerful media empires. Think, The Simpsons, American Idol, Modern Family, and every major sports league imaginable. I’d been on the field at the World Series and the Super Bowl, hosted parties from Las Vegas to the south of France with actors, National Geographic Explorers, and WWE wrestlers.

It was everything I’d never even dreamed of since I dropped out of business school and moved to the West Coast without a career plan over two decades ago.

The network advertising chiefs (what they call the head of ad revenue at the major TV networks) had long held the most powerful jobs in media and advertising. They were rainmakers and ringleaders. They helped shape the ad spending of the world’s largest companies and weave their messages into content people love. They connected marketers with the Hollywood storytellers who offer the opportunity to reach many millions of viewers during their favorite programming in order to hopefully persuade them to buy a new Ford or Toyota, trust Aflac or State Farm with their home or car insurance, reach for Irish Spring or Dove soap in the shower, kick back with a Budweiser or Heineken.

For years, network advertising chief was the biggest job in all advertising. But by the time I got to Fox, the ground was shifting. Networks were consolidating, and TV advertising was shrinking as viewers were opting out of the traditional TV experience. My remit as president of advertising at Fox Networks Group, at least as I described it, was to make the advertising “suck less.” And with a true Quixote-like effort, I tried to do just that right up until Disney acquired (most of) Fox.

When I finally got the call from Disney HR, it confirmed what had long ago been decided: I wasn’t going to become a “cast member” (a.k.a. Disney employee). But that morning in Tokyo, all I could think about was how few people could say they’d been fired twice by mouse-centric companies.

The first time it happened, I was working at Chuck E. Cheese in Latham, New York. I was seventeen years old and, despite the perpetual sweat smell, I actually enjoyed running around in the mouse costume and entertaining kids. And if I am being honest, the real reason I applied there was to get the title of assistant manager.

Considering all the free pizza, getting excellent at Pop-A-Shot (but not Skee-Ball, no matter how many times I played), and the fact that there was always some low stakes human drama to triage, it was everything you could ask for in a high school job: seniority at seventeen and perks galore.

One time, the employee in the Chuck E. outfit was running through the main room and tripped and fell. The giant mouse head came off and rolled across the dining room. Birthday parties watched with various levels of horror or amusement. There were a lot of free pizza and prizes given that day. I loved solving people-problems and dealing with eccentric personalities, and the Latham (that’s actual upstate New York, near Albany) Chuck E. Cheese was never short on either.

But when summer rolled around, I made more money on weekends lifeguarding. So, when I wouldn’t change my schedule, a company whose whole brand identity was a grinning, wise-cracking, anthropomorphic mouse parted ways with me, and not for the last time, it would turn out.

Chuck E. Cheese (Charles Entertainment Cheese, if you’re feeling formal) really brought together all the things I would later come to love: hospitality, iconic IP, entertainment, and games. The term “experiential” hadn’t yet entered my lexicon, but that’s exactly what I loved—live, immersive entertainment that engages people in a way technology has yet to replicate. I didn’t realize it at the time, but the manic energy of Chuck E. Cheese—the unlimited soft drinks and pizza and loud music and video games—was a perfect metaphor for today’s entertainment-centric world of infinite distractions.

The difference is that, at Chuck E. Cheese, the chaos was shared and physical. You were elbow-to-elbow with other people, feeding sticky tokens into machines, celebrating wins together. Today we experience that same sensory overload virtually and alone, our attention splintered by endless notifications and algorithmically generated content, isolated behind screens that promise connection but deliver only the simulation of it.

Attention is the world’s, and every individual’s, most valuable resource, influencing our lives and the planet in ways we’re just beginning to understand. Attention may be finite, but what it can be converted into is not. It shapes everything—not just what we watch and the products we buy—but who we date, whether we marry, the movements we join, the causes we fight for, and even where we worship and how we die.

This idea has shaped my career in media and advertising (theoretically the market for buying and selling attention), giving me a front-row seat to the modern attention wars—how they’ve been won and lost and how they’ve transformed our world over the last twenty-five years.

Today, an astonishing percentage of the global economy—trillions upon trillions of dollars in market valuation—is built on top of algorithms competing to attract, harvest, and monetize attention. Once viewed as the business of brand awareness, a marketing expense, advertising is now the invisible infrastructure of the entire global economy.

Joe Marchese is CEO of Human Ventures Holdings and co-founder and general partner of Casa Komos Brands Group.

articles.title: MSQ Group Acquires January Digital to Build Out Media Offerings
articles.fullContent:
By Lauren Johnson Private equity-backed MSQ Group has acquired media agency January Digital as it looks to grow its U.S. business.

The acquisition gives MSQ a stronger media offering to compete with the large holding companies, said Aaron Lang, U.S. president of MSQ Partners.

London-based MSQ owns agencies including Big Spaceship, Arke, Elmwood , 26PMX, and Forge. Lang said that MSQ has looked to acquire creative, digital experience, and media agencies.

While MSQ offers media services, the U.S. footprint up until now has been “sub-scale” and specific to industries like financial services and professional associations, according to Lang.

“The thing that was really difficult was finding someone who was the right size with the with all of the criteria,” he said. “There’s either the really large scale of the holding companies or there’s parts and pieces—there weren’t a lot of the mid-size.”

Fourteen-year-old January Digital is a media and strategy agency founded by CEO Vic Drabicky. The agency works with brands including Supergoop, Steve Madden, and Amika. January Digital primarily works with retail clients but has diversified its portfolio over the years. Drabicky estimated that 70% of the agency’s clients are retail, down from nearly all clients five years ago.

Supergoop Partners With Target and the PGA Tour as It Chases Mass Appeal Drabicky had been looking for a strategic buyer for more than a year, and landed on MSQ due its financial, business, and cultural fit.

“When you’re an independent, you can only develop at such a certain rate,” he said. “For us, it was about finding a partner who could fill any of the gaps in our services and do it in a way that allowed us to compete with those bigger holding companies.”

January Digital’s leadership team will join MSQ and retain its name as part of the acquisition. MSQ employs 2,000 people globally, with 500 in the U.S.

MSQ’s Lang said the company is potentially looking for smaller acquisitions, adding that January Digital represents a “tentpole acquisition” aimed at winning bigger clients within the U.S.

“We feel that with that acquisition, we’re able to compete with just about anybody,” Lang said.

Lauren Johnson is Adweek's deputy editor of commerce, where she runs Adweek's retail and influencer marketing coverage. Before joining Adweek in 2024, she was an advertising reporter at Business Insider for six years and previously covered technology for Adweek.

articles.title: Google’s Search Antitrust Ruling: What Advertisers Should Check Next
articles.fullContent:
This post was sponsored by Silver Arbitration Law, PLLC. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

If you manage Google Search campaigns, you have explained rising CPCs many times: more competitors, broader match types, a lower Quality Score, an account that needed restructuring. Each explanation is plausible.

I have worked in arbitration since before Google existed, as both counsel and arbitrator. Below I set out what the record shows: what the court found, which auction changes it named and when they ran, and what you would have to establish about your own account before any of it applies to you.

Why The Search Antitrust Ruling Matters For Digital Paid Marketers & Advertisers

In August 2024, after a ten-week trial, the court found that Google “has exercised its monopoly power by charging supracompetitive prices for general search text ads” ( Mem. Op. at 4 ).

Supracompetitive means above the price a competitive market would produce.

The trial record showed that Google’s ads team used internal “ pricing knobs ” that raised what a winning ad paid without any change in bids, ad quality or competition, mostly by inflating the runner-up’s score that sets the winner’s CPC.

Dates Of The Auction Changes That Raised CPCs

Four of these instances have date ranges you can check against your own account:

Format pricing, 2012–2019. Ads using sitelinks, callouts or structured snippets paid more to maintain their position. By 2019 the charges generated about 15% of text ad revenue (UPX0042, UPX0045, UPX0512; Mem. Op. at 84, 86 ; Pls.’ Proposed Findings at 231 ).

Squashing, 2014 onward. Trial exhibits show Google raised the predicted click-through rate of every ad except the leader, which raised the winner’s price without any improvement in the competing ad (UPX0442, UPX0051; Mem. Op. at 83–84 ).

rGSP, 2019 onward. Under rGSP, Google multiplies the runner-up’s score by an adjustable factor; the winner pays against that inflated score or is randomly swapped out of the slot. Projected effect: a 5–6% CPC increase on top slots. No opt-out (UPX1045, UPX0457, UPX0059; Mem. Op. at 85 ; Pls.’ Proposed Findings at 235–236 ).

Advertisers were not told. Google’s Vice President of Ads testified: “We tend not to tell advertisers about pricing changes” ( Tr. 1226, Dischler ). The court found that “[m]any advertisers do not even realize that Google is responsible for the changes in price” ( Mem. Op. at 91–93, 260 ).

Individual advertisers still need to establish whether they were affected and by how much. The first step is to get informed, and there are two ways to do it. You can ask an arbitration lawyer to assess your account; I do this for advertisers, and you can book a short call with me . Or you can read up on the case first: this research prompt has an AI assistant brief you on what the courts found and whether it fits a business like yours.

Start With The Google Ads Spend You Need To Review

The search ruling covers general search text ads. The court did not find a monopoly in the broader market for all search advertising, which includes ads sold by retailers such as Amazon and Walmart. If much of your spend went to Shopping or Performance Max, separate the text-ad portion before drawing conclusions about your account. This research prompt has an AI assistant tell you which ad types and years of spend count.

Clarify The Business & Agency Behind The Account

Note which legal entity accepted Google’s advertising terms and paid the invoices, and which agencies or manager accounts ran the campaigns and when. Those details determine who can review the account and who would raise any claim, and they are the first thing counsel will ask for.

Verify The Court Sources Behind The Search-Ruling Claims

Display spend falls under a second ruling. On April 17, 2025, Judge Leonie Brinkema of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia found that Google had monopolized two parts of the display advertising chain.

That case focused largely on publishers, and the court did not accept every market claim the government brought. If you bought display inventory through Google’s ad tech tools, it raises a separate question about how those transactions worked. Which ruling matters to you depends on the products you used and the years you used them.

Distinguish Findings, Appeals & Unverified Claims

Court findings in this article are quoted with a page cite to the opinion. Anything cited to an exhibit number (UPX, DX) or a transcript (Tr., Dep.) is a trial exhibit or sworn testimony, most of it Google’s own. The two are not the same: a finding is what the court concluded; an exhibit is evidence the court heard.

Google disagrees with the ruling and is appealing . The court’s September 2025 remedies decision requires Google to disclose material changes to its ad auction publicly . Advertisers should therefore have more information about changes that affect what they pay.

Prepare Account-Specific Questions For Counsel

Confirm Applicable Terms, Claim Ownership & Timing

Google’s advertising terms contain an arbitration clause . Advertisers bound by that clause must pursue covered disputes through individual arbitration and waive the right to bring a class action. Each advertiser pursuing such a claim brings it through the American Arbitration Association. The court’s findings provide a starting point; reviewing an account and deciding whether to file remain separate steps.

A claim could be potentially worth 15% to 30% of your eligible search spend. Economists estimate Google’s overcharge at about 5% to 10%, and antitrust law triples proven damages. If your business spent $10 million on eligible search ads during the relevant period, that points to a potential claim of $1.5 million to $3 million, before fees and case-specific adjustments. That is the size of the claim. An arbitrator or a settlement decides what is paid. Could Filing Affect Your Google Account?

Advertisers ask me this more than anything else. Thousands of U.S. advertisers are already pursuing individual claims, and I am not aware of any reported retaliation against one for filing. Retaliating against a group of claimants that size would create a new legal and reputational problem for Google while two federal courts are overseeing its conduct. In my view the practical risk is low. You are also not suing Google: you are using the arbitration process Google wrote into its own advertising terms. Ask your lawyer how the filing is handled and what Google sees. The research prompt guide I’ve put together ends with three questions to put to a lawyer. How Much Work Is It?

Less than most advertisers expect. For a standard claim, gathering and submitting the account records should take about one hour of staff time in total, usually split between someone with access to the Google Ads account and an authorized signatory. After that, your lawyer should handle the assessment, the filing and the coordination, and come back to you only when a decision or case-specific input is needed. If a firm asks for much more of your time than that, ask why. Any time your in-house counsel spends reviewing the engagement is separate and depends on your internal approval process. What If An Agency Manages The Account?

articles.title: ADWEEK Launches Inaugural Creator Economy Power List
articles.fullContent:
ADWEEK has launched and is now accepting entries for the 2026 Creator Economy Power List, honoring the executives building the business behind the creator boom.

While the creators themselves normally get the spotlight, this honor is reserved for the dealmakers, platform builders, brand leaders, and technologists turning the creator business into a durable economy.

Who’s Eligible Entrants must work at a company operating in the creator economy. Individual creators, influencers, and on-camera talent are not eligible unless they are entering for a business role, such as founder or executive of a company. Creators are encouraged to enter ADWEEK Brand Genius Creators.

Creative & Influencer Agencies: Shops that plan, cast, and run creator-led campaigns for brands

Brand-side Marketers: In-house leaders who have made creators a core part of their marketing mix

Social Media Platforms: The companies building the programs, products, and payouts that creators depend on

Content Creation & Management Tools: Software that helps creators and brands make, edit, schedule, and manage content

Talent Management Firms: Managers and agencies representing creators and building their businesses

Creator Monetization Platforms: Companies helping creators earn through subscriptions, commerce, tipping, licensing, and more

Creator Adtech: Measurement, marketplace, data and analytics, and media-buying technology that makes creator content work as a paid channel

Entrants may nominate themselves or a colleague.

What We’re Looking For ADWEEK judges will favor entries that show hard results from the past 12 months, not just vision. Entries with verifiable metrics, named campaigns, and clear timelines will stand out.

Business impact: Revenue growth, funding, new clients, or market share, with numbers wherever possible

Innovation: A new product, model, or partnership that changed how brands and creators work together

Creator Outcomes: Measurable gains for the creators the entrant’s business serves, from earnings to reach

Industry Influence : Leadership that moved the wider market, including standards, deals, or programs others followed

Key Dates & Fees Early Bird Deadline (until November 6) – $175

The final deadline to submit is Monday, December 7, 2026 at 11:59pm PST .

For any questions, please reach out to awards@adweek.com .

articles.title: Dear Media and Amanda Hirsch Want Brands To Ditch the Script
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Stenberg For podcast host Amanda Hirsch, the best brand partnerships start before a deal is ever signed.

Hirsch, who hosts Not Skinny But Not Fat, will even accept a lower fee from a brand she already uses, she told ADWEEK chief content officer Zoe Ruderman at ADWEEK’s Advertising HQ event.

Hirsch runs every potential partner through a few filters: whether she’s an organic fan, whether she has tried the product herself, and whether her audience would find it genuinely useful. Turning down a deal is not painful, she added, because she believes another opportunity will follow.

“I’m thinking about my audience, like, ‘Wait, they would love this,’” Hirsch said. “‘This would be so helpful for them.'”

That approach fits the model at Dear Media, which has a roster of about 100 shows and a sales team of roughly 40 people. The company rarely runs programmatic advertising, relying instead on host-read ads that talent can shape directly with the brand, according to Mark Mullett, Dear Media’s president of global entertainment.

In fact, the biggest mistake brands still make is handing talent a script and expecting them to read it, according to Mullett. Another misconception is that creators will take any offer for the money, he added.

“Let creators create,” he said. “If they said yes to working with a brand, let them cook, let them do their thing. It’s going to be better for you.”

The strategy appears to be working. Last year, Dear Media was on track to generate between $50 million and $100 million in revenue, after having raised around $12 million in investment, according to The New York Times .

Video has widened what those partnerships look like, from product placement on set to IRL events and footage spliced into episodes. For instance, Dear Media recently worked with Weight Watchers, a partnership that included a show hosted by a company employee about her own GLP-1 journey. The show focuses less on the science than on the psychological and personal side of the experience.

While the phrase “brand entertainment” can be a little “snoozy,” the concept behind it is sound, per Mullett.

“It’s really just great entertainment—brought to you by Weight Watchers,” he said.

Hirsch, for her part, mostly avoids the numbers, checking performance only when quarterly reports arrive. She considers an episode a success when listeners walk away loving a guest they had never heard of before.

Her dream partner, after years of organically talking about the brand: Ugg.

Mark Stenberg is ADWEEK's senior media reporter.

articles.title: Google Opens Search Profiles In India & Canada, Brazil Next via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
Google is opening Search profiles to creators and publishers in India and Canada. Until today, the profiles were only open in the U.S., where they launched in June.

Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, announced the expansion on X. Search profiles are claimable pages that pull a source’s articles and social posts together.

“One of our most requested updates for Search profiles is live today: expanding to new countries!”

He wrote that creators and publishers in India and Canada can now “set up their own dedicated home base on Google,” with Brazil “rolling out soon.”

In an Aug. 12 X post about lowering the follower thresholds, he wrote, “We’ll also expand them to more countries soon.” When Google cut the threshold again on Sept. 16, the announcement named only U.S. publishers and creators, as I reported then .

Google’s help page for creating a profile still listed only the U.S. at midday Oct. 6, after Stein’s post went up. It said:

“Search profiles are currently only available in the United States.”

The page required at least one platform, YouTube, Instagram, X, or TikTok, to have 10,000 followers, and the person creating the profile had to be at least 18. Stein’s post does not clarify whether this follower requirement applies in India and Canada.

The page’s setup involves visiting profile.google.com/claim , signing in with the desired Google Account, and linking at least one platform account that meets the follower minimum the page listed.

A Canadian or Indian publication now has the opportunity to set up a Search profile, the page U.S. sources have had since June. Google’s help page explains that creating a profile doesn’t directly impact a source’s ranking in Google Search. However, followers of the profile may see more of that source’s content in Discover.

Brazil is upcoming for Search profiles, although Google’s Robby Stein didn’t provide a specific date. Stein’s announcement mentions that setup in India and Canada begins today, so you can try it out on the claim page.

articles.title: Data Shows Which Negative Search Results Can Actually Be Removed via @sejournal, @EraseDotCom
articles.fullContent:
This post was sponsored by Erase . The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

Say a client sends you five links. There’s a Google review, a Yelp review, a republished court record, a Reddit thread, and a local news story. Which ones can come down?

Going by our 2026 data, an eligible Google review and a republished court record usually can. The Yelp review, the Reddit thread, and the news story are more difficult.

Negative content can also appear in AI-generated answers . Our May analysis for SEJ found AI Overviews showing negative reviews in searches that didn’t ask for them. That makes it useful to know which sources are likely to remove content and which require a different approach.

Negative Search Results: What 2026 Removal Data Shows

We looked at 22,620 links clients sent to Erase.com between January 1 and September 21, 2026. They came from about 1,650 websites, and the results split sharply by site.

In this analysis, a successful removal could mean taking a page down, de-indexing it, or removing the client’s name or photo. De-indexing keeps a page out of Google’s search results without taking it offline.

What People Asked To Remove: Google Reviews Led

Google reviews made up about half of the links in the category breakdown. That breakdown excludes the image-heavy case described in the methodology.

More than 1,000 websites showed up only once in the data. News links alone came from 708 different outlets, each with its own editors and rules.

Easier To Remove: Eligible Google Reviews

Google reviews came down more reliably than almost anything else we handled.

Google lists the reviews it will remove in its prohibited and restricted content policy . The list includes fake reviews, impersonation, harassment, off-topic posts, and personal information. When a review clearly fits one of those, Google usually takes it down.

Fastest To Remove: Court Records, Mugshots & People-Search Listings

Republished court records, mugshots, and people-search listings were the most reliable categories and the fastest to remove. The median removal in each took less than two weeks.

Harder To Remove: Yelp Reviews, Reddit Threads & News Stories

Reviews on Yelp, Trustpilot, Indeed, BBB, and Glassdoor rarely came down. Reddit threads and news stories were also harder to remove.

How Long Successful Content Removals Took

For successful outcomes, the median time was 18 days. Of those, 71% were confirmed within 30 days and 91% within 90 days. These figures describe how long successful outcomes took, not the likelihood that a submitted link would be removed.

Content type Median days to removal Removed within 30 days Court records 9 89% People-search listings 9 84% Mugshots 11 93% Social media posts 14 79% Google reviews 19 67% News articles 28 51% All removals 18 71% Full removals were faster than de-indexing, at a median of 14 days versus 21.

Some successful Google review removals took much longer. About one in 10 took more than 90 days, so don’t give up on a report after a month.

How To Remove Negative Search Results By Source

Use these findings to set expectations, then follow the removal route that matches each source.

Step 1: Group Negative Search Results By Source

Group your negative links by website, then check each site’s rules and removal options. Start with the sites that move fast, like court-record and people-search sites. If removal or de-indexing isn’t available, plan to push the link down in search instead.

Choose the route that matches each link’s source: Google reviews | Yelp and other reviews | Court records | Mugshots and people-search | Social posts | News, Reddit and government pages .

Before reporting a Google review, check the platform’s policies and the legal limits on removal requests. The FTC’s Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect in October 2024. It bars businesses from using threats, intimidation, or false accusations to get a review removed.

Check Whether The Google Review Violates Policy

Find the policy the review breaks. A review that is not based on a genuine experience can qualify. A harsh but honest review usually doesn’t. This page covers which Google reviews can be removed .

Report The Google Review, Then Appeal If Needed

articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Engagement rate measures how many people interact with your social content relative to reach, impressions, or follower count. It includes actions like likes, comments, shares, and saves, but not passive views.
  2. The most common formula is engagement rate by reach (ERR): total engagements divided by reach, multiplied by 100. Different formulas suit different goals, from organic posts to paid campaigns.
  3. A good engagement rate typically falls between 1% and 5%, but benchmarks vary significantly by platform and industry. Always compare against your specific platform and industry, not a universal standard.
  4. Tracking engagement rate over time shows which content resonates, which formats to prioritize, and where to adjust your strategy. Perch by Hootsuite automates that tracking across all your accounts, and social media analytics tools can also provide industry benchmarks for comparison.

What is engagement rate?

Engagement rate is a social media metric that measures how much of your audience actively engages with your content. It defines the amount of interaction a piece of content (or a campaign, or a whole account) gets compared to reach or audience size.

Engagement metrics vary by channel, but in general, it’s any action someone takes to interact with your content, including likes, comments, shares, saves, poll responses, messages, or link clicks. Because each platform counts engagement a little differently, it helps to know exactly what actions feed into your social media engagement rate before you calculate it.

Why does engagement rate matter?

Engagement rate matters because it shows whether your content is actually connecting with your audience. When people take the time to like, comment, share, or save a post, it’s a strong signal that they find it interesting or useful.

Second, higher engagement rates help you get better visibility on social media platforms. That’s because social algorithms surface more engaging content to new audiences.

A lot of engagement on your content also makes you look more trustworthy and appealing to first-time profile visitors, especially if there’s an active conversation happening in your comments. For enterprise teams, engagement rate is also one of the clearest ways to prove social ROI to leadership, since it ties content performance to real audience behavior.

What counts as engagement on each platform?

Engagement is any action a user takes to interact with your content, but the specific actions that count vary from platform to platform. Knowing what feeds into the formula helps you calculate an accurate engagement rate and compare performance fairly across channels.

Here’s what typically counts as engagement on each major social network:

  • Instagram: Likes, comments, shares, saves, and replies to Stories.
  • TikTok: Likes, comments, shares, saves, and follows generated by a video.
  • Facebook: Reactions, comments, shares, and clicks on links or buttons.
  • LinkedIn: Reactions, comments, shares (reposts), and clicks.
  • X (Twitter): Likes, replies, reposts, quote posts, and clicks.
  • Pinterest: Saves (repins), comments, clicks, and close-ups.

Passive metrics like impressions and views usually don’t count as engagement on their own, since they measure exposure rather than interaction. When in doubt, check the platform’s analytics to confirm which actions it includes before running your numbers.

How to calculate engagement rate (6 formulas)

The standard engagement rate formula is total engagements divided by reach, multiplied by 100. That said, there are six variations worth knowing, because each one uses a different denominator and answers a slightly different question.

  1. Engagement rate by reach (ERR): Most common.
  2. Engagement rate by post (ER post): Best for specific posts.
  3. Engagement rate by impressions (ER impressions): Best for paid content.
  4. Daily engagement rate (Daily ER): Best for long-term analysis.
  5. Engagement rate by views (ER views): Best for video.
  6. Cost per engagement (CPE): Best for influencer marketing or conversion-based campaigns.

1. Engagement rate by reach (ERR): Most common

This is the most common engagement rate formula. ERR measures the percentage of people who interact with your content after seeing it.

Here’s how to calculate engagement rate for a single post:

ERR = total number of engagements on a post / reach of that post * 100

To calculate the average ERR across multiple posts, add together the ERR for each post and divide by the total number of posts:

Average ERR = Total ERR / Number of posts

For example: Post 1 (3.4%) + Post 2 (3.5%) / 2 = 3.45%

Pros: Because not all followers see every post, ERR is often more accurate than follower-based metrics, especially in algorithm-driven feeds. Reach includes both followers and non-followers who discover content through search, shares, hashtags, and recommendations.

Cons: Reach can fluctuate for a variety of reasons, making it a difficult variable to control. ...

articles.title: Layoffs on the Way as Skydance Now Controls Paramount and WBD
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro David Ellison has finally brought together Paramount Skydance properties and Warner Bros. Discovery properties under the same roof, creating a new conglomerate, Skydance. And cuts will follow as the companies consolidate.

The merger officially closed Tuesday morning, with CEO Ellison and his co-CEO, Ynon Kreiz , celebrating the moment with staffers and saying that under Skydance, creating great stories will be at the heart of “everything we do.”

Paramount Studios, Warner Bros. Studios, HBO, HBO Max, Paramount+, CBS, CBS Sports, TBS, TNT, CNN, Pluto TV, Discovery, MTV, BET, Nickelodeon, and many other linear channels will now fall under one single umbrella.

Getting to this point did not come without drama, as Ellison had to wrestle WBD away from Netflix in early 2026 , which initially had sought to acquire Warner Bros. Studios, with the linear properties being left to create a new entity.

To win the merger, Paramount offered what WBD called a “superior” bid , which included an all-cash offer of $31 per share.

After that, various state attorneys general, along with the Writers Guild of America, filed a lawsuit seeking to block the merger, which was ultimately settled in September and came with movie production guarantees and an independent board ensuring editorial independence for CNN and CBS News.

The new conglomerate will come with roughly $80 billion in debt, which the company must now work to pay down. Unfortunately, one of the easiest ways of accomplishing this is through layoffs.

Ellison and Kreiz acknowledged future cuts in a statement saying, “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce. We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully.”

articles.title: Here Are the 3rd Quarter of 2026 Cable News Ratings
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro Below are the cable news ratings for the third quarter of 2026.

The summer period was not kind to all the cable news networks, as hot, sunny weather combined with a slow news period led to quarter-to-quarter declines in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo during primetime and total day.

Fox News, MS NOW, and CNN finished with double-digit losses in both measured categories across the two observed dayparts.

Despite this, Fox News remained the most-watched cable network during this period. It hopes to carry that momentum into the last quarter, which will be sports-heavy programming-wise but, on the news front, will include consequential midterm elections.

According to Nielsen big data + panel, Fox News averaged 2.064 million total primetime viewers and 183,000 Adults 25-54 viewers in Q3 2026. During total day, Fox News had 1.321 million total viewers and 121,000 demo viewers.

Compared to the second quarter , Fox News was down -17% in total viewers and -20% in the demo during primetime. When looking at total day, it was also down by -16% and -19% in total viewers and the demo, respectively.

Looking at Fox News’ performance against the same quarter in 2025 , total viewers were down -17%, and the demo was down -25% during primetime. In total day, it also fell -16% in total viewers and -24% in the demo, and it was the only network in this yearly comparison to record declines.

Fox News finished the quarter in first place among all cable networks during primetime in total viewers and ranked No. 2 in the demo. During total day, Fox News was again on top in total viewers and finished in second place in the demo.

During Q3 2026, MS NOW averaged 933,000 total primetime viewers and 84,000 primetime demo viewers. During total day, MS NOW had 592,000 total viewers and 56,000 A25-54 viewers.

When looking at MS NOW’s performance vs. the second quarter in 2026, it was down in total viewers and the demo by -12% and -21%, respectively, during primetime. During total day, the network was also down by -10% in total viewers and -16% in the demo.

Looking at its performance vs. the third quarter of 2025, MS NOW was up +16% in total viewers and +27% in the demo during primetime. It was also up +20% in total viewers and +37% in the demo during total day—the only network with gains in both dayparts within this yearly comparison.

MS NOW remained in third place in total viewers and was 16th in the demo. During total day, MS NOW moved to second place from third in total viewers and remained in 10th place in the demo.

CNN averaged 608,000 total primetime viewers and 101,000 primetime demo viewers in Q3 2026. During total day, the network had 426,000 total viewers and 61,000 A25-54 viewers.

Compared with the second quarter, CNN saw drops of -14% in total viewers and -16% in the demo in primetime. Looking at how it performed during total day, it fell by -14% in total viewers and -19% in the demo.

When looking at its performance to the same quarter in 2025 during primetime, it was up +13% in total viewers and +16% in the demo. In total day, CNN grew +8% in total viewers and was flat in the demo.

CNN slid from fourth place to fifth in primetime among total viewers and was 10th in the demo, tied with FX. During total day, CNN remained in the No. 4 spot in total viewers and was No. 8 in the demo.

articles.title: Holiday shopping is happening earlier than ever, here’s what brands need to know
articles.fullContent:
Halloween candy is still on the shelves, but holiday shoppers are making wish lists and hunting for deals months before the holidays arrive.

But as the shopping season gets longer, budgets are getting tighter. For brands, that means more chances to get in front of consumers, but also more competition for every dollar shoppers spend.

Data from Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey points to three factors that will define the holiday season: campaign timing, price sensitivity and meeting shoppers where they’re increasingly discovering gifts—on social.

Consumers don’t want earlier holiday campaigns, except when they do

Consumers have mixed feelings about how early holiday marketing should start.

According to Sprout’s Q3 2026 pulse survey, nearly half (49%) say campaigns launched as early as August make them more likely to buy, including 19% who say they’re much more likely. Just 11% say an early start makes them less likely to purchase.

But ask consumers when brands should launch their holiday campaigns and the story changes. Half point to October or November as the ideal window, compared to 21% who prefer August or September. Another 12% say brands should wait until December.

Those findings may seem contradictory, but they point to a distinction between when consumers want holiday marketing to dominate their feeds and when they’re open to discovering seasonal products. Shoppers can be receptive to gift ideas, new products and seasonal inspiration well before they want brands to go all-in on holiday messaging. In other words, an earlier presence can influence what they eventually buy without making it feel like the holiday season starts in late summer.

The sweet spot: Show up early without going all-in. Use August and September to build awareness and consideration, then ramp up your holiday campaign in October and November.

For example:

  • Tease what’s coming: Preview holiday collections, seasonal launches or upcoming offers.
  • Get gift-worthy products on shoppers’ radar: Introduce products consumers might want to add to their lists before they’re ready to buy.
  • Start publishing seasonal content: Share gift inspiration and other useful holiday content that gives shoppers a reason to engage early.

Starting earlier gives you more room to test what resonates before peak shopping begins. Then you can put more support behind the products, messages and offers gaining traction.

Brands are already putting this approach into practice. Fenty Beauty, for example, launched its limited-edition holiday collection in September, giving shoppers an early look at its seasonal products. As of writing, the TikTok has received over 100K views and over 5K likes.

For years, public relations and SEO have operated in neighboring but often separate parts of the marketing organization. AI search is beginning to change that relationship.

As AI systems become a larger part of how people discover companies, products, and services, the sources those systems rely on are becoming increasingly important. Third-party coverage from trusted publications can provide information that helps establish a brand’s credibility and authority.
That shift is changing how organizations think about digital PR.
New industry projections suggest PR budgets could double by 2027 as brands respond to the growing importance of AI-powered search. The underlying reason is straightforward: brands need to be visible in the places AI systems use to understand and evaluate them.
For marketers, that makes earned media more than a traditional awareness channel. Consistent third-party coverage can contribute to a brand’s broader search presence while strengthening the information available about it across the web.

Why AI Search Is Increasing the Value of Digital PR

AI search changes how people encounter information. Instead of receiving a list of links and deciding which ones to visit, users can receive a synthesized answer based on information gathered from multiple sources.

That creates a new role for third-party coverage.

AI Systems Rely on Trusted Sources

AI systems need information they can retrieve and use when generating answers.

A company’s own website is an important source, but it isn’t the only one. News publications, industry websites, reviews, research organizations, and other third-party sources can provide additional context about a brand. Academic databases are a great example.

This is where earned media becomes valuable.

A company that is consistently mentioned by credible publications creates a broader information footprint than one that relies primarily on its own website. Those mentions can help reinforce what the company does, who its experts are, and where it has authority.

That doesn’t guarantee an AI system will cite any particular article. It does create more opportunities for a brand’s information to exist within the sources AI systems may encounter.

Authority is difficult to establish through a single piece of coverage.

One major publication can create awareness, but its effect can fade. A sustained presence across relevant publications creates a different type of signal.

Repeated coverage can reinforce the same core facts about a business across multiple sources. Over time, this can contribute to stronger brand recognition and a clearer understanding of the company’s expertise.

For AI visibility, that consistency matters because AI systems are constantly processing information from across the web.

The temptation in PR has often been to measure success by the biggest placement a campaign can generate. A marquee publication can certainly be valuable, but it shouldn’t be the only objective.

Credibility Compounds Over Time

A single article can introduce a company to a new audience. An ongoing stream of relevant coverage can keep reinforcing the brand.

You can use Claude to create or publish social media content on platforms like Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, Twitter/X, and more.

articles.title: What’s Making AI Impact Difficult to Measure for Marketers?
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Brands recommended by ChatGPT were 2.5x more likely to receive a website visit within seven days, according to Similarweb research.
  • Most AI-influenced visits did not arrive through an identifiable AI referral.
  • More than half of AI-influenced visits arrived through search, meaning the AI influence can look like ordinary organic traffic in analytics.
  • Last-click attribution can therefore underestimate the role AI plays in brand discovery and consideration.
  • Marketers need broader measurement frameworks that account for AI’s influence across the customer journey.

AI search is becoming an increasingly important way for consumers to discover brands. But measuring its impact is proving much harder than measuring a traditional referral.

A user might ask ChatGPT for a product recommendation, see a brand mentioned, and then search for that brand on Google several days later. Analytics will record the eventual visit, but it may have no way of knowing that an AI recommendation helped start the journey.

New research from Similarweb highlights the scale of this measurement gap. Brands recommended by ChatGPT were 2.5x more likely to receive a website visit within the following seven days, even when there was no direct referral from the AI platform.

The finding suggests that AI visibility can influence traffic without appearing as AI traffic in a standard analytics report.

For marketers, that’s an important distinction. If AI is influencing customers before they reach a website, measuring only the final click can make the channel look less valuable than it actually is.

What Similarweb Found About AI’s Downstream Impact

Similarweb’s research tracked real user journeys to understand what happens after a brand is recommended in ChatGPT.

Source

AI Recommendations Can Lead to More Website Visits</h3>

Similarweb followed users who asked ChatGPT an industry-related question and received a specific brand recommendation. It then tracked their behavior over the following seven days.

Across finance, travel, and beauty, users who received an AI recommendation for a brand were 2.5x more likely to visit that brand’s website than users who received a recommendation for a competing brand.

The research focused on users who had not previously visited the recommended brand and had not already mentioned that brand in their prompt. This helped Similarweb measure the downstream effect of a recommendation rather than simply tracking people who already knew about a company.

The result provides a useful signal for marketers investing in AI visibility. Being mentioned in an AI answer can influence what consumers do afterward, even when the AI platform doesn’t send the eventual website visit.

Most of the Traffic Doesn’t Look Like AI Traffic

This is where traditional measurement becomes complicated.

Similarweb found that 55.9% of AI-influenced visits arrived through search, compared with 40.4% of visits without AI influence.

In practice, that means a user could see a brand recommendation in ChatGPT, remember the name, and later search for it on Google.

That visit would likely be attributed to organic search.

The AI interaction that helped create the interest would receive no credit.

This is the core AI attribution problem. The measurable traffic is real, but the original source of influence can disappear somewhere between discovery and conversion.

Source

Why Last-Click Attribution Misses AI’s Influence

Last-click attribution works reasonably well when a customer journey is relatively direct. But discovery through AI can introduce additional steps that aren’t captured by traditional referral reporting.

The AI Interaction Happens Before the Measurable Visit

Consider a simple journey.

A consumer asks an AI platform which software tools are best for their business. The platform recommends a brand. The consumer doesn’t click a link. Instead, they continue researching, then return to Google two days later and search for the brand by name.

From an analytics perspective, the final visit may look like a branded organic search.

From the customer’s perspective, however, the journey started with AI.

articles.title: Data storytelling: Turning social insights into a narrative your org acts on
articles.fullContent:
Engagement is up. Your brand is seeing a spike in mentions. Sentiment is trending positive. People are sharing a hack about one of your new products. They’re all positive signs, but if you can’t translate what they mean to the business, those numbers stay trapped and nothing changes off the back of that good momentum.

That’s where social teams find themselves stuck. The data they have access to is often the freshest, most unfiltered view of what the market is actually saying, filled with unprompted takes and reactions from the world’s largest focus group. But according to the 2026 Social Intelligence Report, only 36% of organizations are able to use those insights to regularly inform decisions outside of marketing.

That’s when a data problem becomes a storytelling problem. Building a narrative around the data and helping people understand why it matters, and what it means to them, is crucial to help insights from social have an actual business impact.

So what makes a story land? How do you visualize data and shape it into something that drives a recommendation? Below, we’ll cover what data storytelling means for social teams specifically, the building blocks of how to make those stories resonate and a step-by-step framework for putting one together, as well as what to avoid.

What is data storytelling?

Data storytelling is the practice of merging data science, narrative and visualization to give life to the insights in a dashboard, honing in on what they mean and why decision-makers should care. In short, it’s translating the numbers in a spreadsheet into a compelling story, which ultimately leads to a decision being made.

Social is a prime source for this kind of data storytelling, as it offers market intelligence for the business. Every other data source (including CRM records, support tickets, pipeline reports, etc.) reflects what customers do once they’re already actively engaged with you in some way. Social captures live reactions from a much wider audience, with unprompted takes that show up there before anywhere else. A spike in comments questioning a pricing decision or a wave of praise for a feature being deprecated is a story that should be told across the business, not sitting in a dashboard.

Social listening and other tactics can help you find those signals, but shaping them into a story that makes the rest of the business sit up and take notice is where data storytelling comes in.

Why data storytelling matters more than ever

Being able to translate insights into something people can take into their decision making is a key skill for teams that work cross functionally, like the social team. Though the same data is the basis for every narrative, each team wants it packaged differently, as a story that’s relevant to them, and being able to act as that translation layer increases any team’s influence.

For example, executives naturally lean on quantitative data because there’s an easy map to the bottom line. Some of that might be a data problem, but much of it is a governance problem. The insight exists but isn’t getting to other teams, or it was never shaped into a narrative a decision-maker could act on before it was too late.

That’s why data storytelling is so important. It’s more than a visualization of data, it’s the narrative that helps define how to improve the business.

  • Match the format to how it’s being received. A dense report table works fine in a document; it will rarely land in a live presentation.

Give it a narrative arc

The most memorable data stories follow a familiar shape: set the scene, introduce the obstacle, hit the climax and land on a resolution. Applied to a social report, that might look like: here’s where we started, here’s what changed and why, here’s the turning point in the data, and here’s what it means going forward. That structure is what makes people remember the story after they leave the room—and repeat it accurately when they explain it to someone else.

Social media image sizes seem to change… a lot. And using the wrong dimensions can hurt reach, engagement, and brand consistency. 

This guide covers the current image size requirements for every major social platform in 2026.

Key takeaways

  1. Most social platforms still work best with images that are 1080 pixels wide, especially for feed and full-screen formats.
  2. Vertical, mobile-first aspect ratios like 4:5 and 9:16 now outperform square images on most networks.
  3. Tools like Perch by Hootsuite support network-specific resizing, making it easier for teams to stay consistent as specs change.

Quick social media image sizes

We go into more detail for every single network below, but this image includes the social media image sizes you probably look up most often.

Basic Instagram image sizes

  • Profile photo: 320 x 320 px
  • Landscape: 1080 x 566 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1350 px
  • Square: 1080 x 1080
  • Stories and Reels: 1080 x 1920

Basic Facebook image sizes

  • Profile photo: 196 x 196 px
  • Landscape: 1080 x 566 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1359 px
  • Square: 1080 x 1080 px
  • Stories and Reels: 1080 x 1920 px
  • Cover photo: 851 x 315 px

Basic X (formerly Twitter) image sizes

  • Profile photo: 400 x 400 px
  • Landscape: 1280 x 720 px
  • Vertical: 720 x 1280 px
  • Square: 720 x 720 px
  • Cover photo: 1500 x 500 px

Basic LinkedIn image sizes

  • Profile photo: 400 x 400 px
  • Landscape: 1200 x 627 px
  • Vertical: 720 x 900 px
  • Square: 1200 x 1200 px
  • Cover photo size: 1128 x 191 px

Basic TikTok image sizes

  • Profile photo: 20 x 20 px
  • Landscape (ad): 1920 x 1080 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1920 px
  • Square (ad): 640 x 640 px
  • Stories: 1080 x 1920 px

Instagram image sizes

Instagram supports horizontally and vertically oriented images well as square images. Well, sort of. You can still use all of these photo orientations in your posts, and that’s how they’ll appear in the Instagram feed. But they will all be displayed with a vertical crop on your Instagram grid.

This makes image dimensions a little tricky to get right, especially if you want to control the look of your grid as a cohesive whole. Follow these guidelines to make sure your images end up looking their best.

Instagram profile picture size: 320 x 320 pixels

Instagram profile photos are displayed at 110 x 100 pixels, but the image files are stored at 320 x 320 pixels, so make sure to upload an image that’s at least that big.

Even though the dimensions are in a square format, Instagram profile photos are displayed as a circle. Make sure any elements you want to focus on in the photo are centered so they don’t get cropped out.

Instagram post sizes:

  • Landscape image: 1080 x 566 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Vertical image: 1080 x 1350 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Square image: 1080 x 1080 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Carousel images: 1080 x 1350 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Supported aspect ratios: Anywhere between 1.91:1 and 4:5 (feed) / 3:4 (grid)
  • Recommended image size: Width of 1080 pixels, height between 566 and 1350 pixels

Tips:

  • If you want your images to look their best on Instagram, aim to upload an image that is 1080 pixels wide.
  • When you share an Instagram image that’s sized over 1080 pixels, Instagram will size it down to 1080 pixels.
  • If you share a photo that has a resolution lower than 320 pixels, Instagram will size it up to 320 pixels.
  • If your image is between 320 and 1080 pixels wide, Instagram will keep that photo at its original resolution, “as long as the photo’s aspect ratio is between 1.91:1 and 4:5 (a height between 566 and 1350 pixels with a width of 1080 pixels).”
  • If you upload an image using a different ratio, the platform will automatically crop your photo to fit a supported ratio.
  • Remember that all photos appear in vertical format on your grid.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Sentiment and online reputation don’t drive AI citations the way most brands assume. Some data even shows a negative correlation.
  • Format isn’t the deciding factor. 64 percent of AI citations come from ordinary pages, not listicle, how to, or comparison content.
  • On commercial-intent prompts, 82 percent of citations go to third parties and just 3 percent to owned pages.
  • Owned citations, where an AI/LLM result goes to a link directly on your domain, delivered the single strongest visibility lift in the data.
  • Despite new AI model releases causing volatility, inconsistent AI search visibility from one quarter to the next is usually a brand problem, not a platform problem. Brands that win on one AI platform tend to win on all of them.

At brightonSEO 2026, I presented AI search visibility research built from 9 million AI answers across 9 platforms and 400+ enterprise brands, the same dataset behind this piece. The feedback I got from conference attendees  in the days that followed made one thing clear: most of what marketers assume about AI search visibility hasn’t actually been tested against real data.

This comes from real client and competitor data tracked across a wealth of company times, from ecommerce to finance to B2B software,. 

Nine assumptions keep showing up in GEO pitches, LinkedIn posts, and Slack threads, and none of them hold up once you check them against this data. Fundamentals beat hacks, and data beats opinion. Here’s what actually drives AI citations, and what to do differently for your GEO strategy starting now.

Myth 1: Positive Sentiment Drives More AI Citations

A lot of ORM budgets are allocated in 2026 based on the idea that better reviews and healthier brand sentiment should earn a brand more AI citations.

The data says otherwise. Across five major platforms, ChatGPT, AI Mode, Gemini, Copilot, and Grok, sentiment correlates negatively or flat with citation frequency. Brands with rockier reputations often get cited more, not less.

The likely mechanism: these models retrieve based on how often and how deeply a brand gets discussed, not on how people feel about it. Controversy generates more discussion than a quiet, well-liked brand ever does, and more discussion means more material for a model to pull from when it builds an answer.

Stop treating AI visibility as a reputation-management outcome. If you’re funding ORM work hoping it moves your citation count, it likely won’t, at least not directly. Sentiment still matters for conversion, trust, and E-E-A-T, so keep investing in it. Just don’t expect it to explain your AI visibility numbers. 

Myth 2: Listicles, Comparisons, and How-Tos Win the Most AI Citations

“Structure it as a listicle and AI will cite you” has become the default logic behind a lot of “AI-optimized” content briefs.

64 percent of AI citations actually come from ordinary pages, not those formats.

The reason: these models pull whichever passage best answers the prompt, format aside. A thorough category page or a detailed guide often answers more prompts than a thin, formulaic list built only to be cited.

Stop treating AI optimization as a formatting exercise. Make your regular pages more thorough instead, with better question coverage, more specifics, and original data the model can actually pull from.

Myth 3: Your Transactional Pages Control Your Transactional Prompts

Who knows a product better than the company selling it? That logic is why so many brands assume their own product and pricing pages would carry the most weight on their commercial-intent prompts.

On commercial-intent prompts, 82 percent of citations go to third parties. Owned pages make up just 3 percent, compared to as much as 13 percent owned coverage on navigational and informational queries.

At the exact moment someone is deciding whether to spend money, these models default to treating any source other than the seller as more credible. At 3% of citations, it seems your own pricing page is the last place they look for confirmation.

Aim digital PR investment specifically at bottom-of-funnel, commercial-intent topics — pricing comparisons, category roundups, best-for placements — rather than only top-funnel awareness moments.

articles.title: How to get ahead of the holiday social media customer service rush with Sprout
articles.fullContent:
Holiday shoppers no longer line up outside big-box stores for the best deals. Instead, they’re turning to social media to find, research and buy gifts. And when their shopping experience falls short, social is where they go to ask questions and share their frustrations.

Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey shows that this holiday season, 86% of consumers plan to use social media for customer service as much (59%) or more (27%) than they did in 2025. As the peak shopping season approaches, social customer service volumes are likely to rise along with holiday demand.

To keep things running smoothly, customer care teams must make the most of all available resources. Luckily, Sprout Social is equipped with tools designed to alleviate the holiday rush while strengthening customer relationships—a gift that keeps on giving well after the holiday season.

‘Tis the season to bolster your customer care strategy. Keep reading to shape your strategy and to find out which Sprout features will set your team and customers up for success during this crucial holiday period.

Why social needs to be at the center of holiday customer service

Answering customer questions on social sits firmly in the center of the social media and customer care Venn diagram.

Social media is a direct line to your customers. And during the busy holiday season, their outreach will inevitably increase, further cementing social’s role in the entire customer journey.

Let’s look at three key ways social media must be central to your holiday customer service.

Social is the home of product discovery

“TikTok made me buy it” is more than a catchy phrase. It’s a reflection of the influence social media has on buying behavior—on TikTok and beyond.

Social media is a virtual mall designed for product discovery, social proof and purchasing all in one place—and its popularity is only growing. In the Q3 2026 Sprout Social Pulse Survey, social media tied with retail stores as the #1 resource for gift ideas and product discovery, with 46% of respondents saying they plan to use social media to find gifts.

Compared to last year, 28% of all consumers plan to use social more to find holiday gift ideas, and 50% plan to use it just as much.

These figures are even higher among Millennials and Gen Z. Specifically, 85% of Millennials plan to use social as much or more for gift research in 2026. And the vast majority of Gen Z (88%) fall into the same boat.

To stay relevant during the holiday season, customer service must prioritize social media, meeting shoppers at the heart of their gift search. Outfitting your team with the training and social media customer care tools they need boosts customer satisfaction by resolving issues where they’re most active.

Customer outreach on social will surge during the holiday season

Many brands, especially those in hospitality and retail, can expect to see an increase in customer queries and requests throughout the festive season. And knowing where and how those messages will come in is critical to your seasonal success.

Per the Q3 2026 pulse survey, users who contact brands on social media still overwhelmingly prefer direct messaging, with 55% of participants naming it as their channel of choice when reaching out to a brand on social media. Other popular communication methods include posting comments, tagging a company publicly or replying to a story.

This spike in outreach could be linked to the fact that consumers are increasingly using social platforms’ built-in shopping capabilities. Some of the most popular include TikTok Shop, Instagram Checkout and Facebook Marketplace. When asked if they plan to make a purchase directly within a social media app this festive season, more than half (57%) of participants said yes. Of that, 38% said they have already done so and 19% said they would try it for the first time.

Having visibility and access to social is crucial for delivering strong customer service. If customer care teams are only reviewing and responding to email, phone and web form requests, they’re not getting the full picture of holiday-time customer service needs.

Consumers reach out on social during every step of their shopping journey

From inquiring about restocks to posting reviews, customers engage with social media at every stage of their shopping journey.

And when it comes to contacting brands, consumers have network preferences. The top channels and the proportion of consumers likely to use them are as follows:

  • TikTok – 50%
  • Facebook – 46%
  • Instagram – 44%
  • Bluesky – 36%
  • Signal – 35%
  • X – 28%
  • Snapchat – 26%

With this data in mind, your team needs access to, and if necessary, training on engaging through these channels.

Remember: A stellar holiday customer service strategy doesn’t just resolve issues—it can turn casual shoppers into loyal customers and enthusiastic advocates. At the same time, a strategy that doesn’t account for social has the power to do the opposite.

10 tips to improve your customer service during the holidays

With the right toolkit and strategic processes, you can take the holiday season from stressful to streamlined.

If you want to revisit and revise your procedures before the rush hits, here are 10 tips for enhancing your holiday customer service strategy. Plus, we’ll explore some ways Sprout can help along the way.

1. Plan ahead

The holidays feel like they start earlier every year. If you’re not planning for the holiday shopping surge—by organizing your team, prepping for a Black Friday social media campaign and solidifying influencer partnerships—you’re risking the chaos of last-minute adjustments.

This year, avoid the scramble of catching up in a busy season. Plan to ensure smooth sailing before the ‘season’s greetings’ decor goes up.

Consider the other milestones your agents should align with—think: key dates for holiday marketing, like Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales or the last shipping days for guaranteed holiday delivery, that may lead to a spike in messages.

Teams should also be conscious of the challenges consumers face this time of year. For instance, the 2025 Deloitte Holiday Retail Survey found that 58% of people consider holiday shopping to be stressful. Financial strain is a key contributor for consumers this year, too, with the Q3 2026 pulse survey finding that 56% of consumers plan to reduce spending.

Although a well-oiled customer care process may not solve these problems, it can relieve stress on already overwhelmed shoppers.

Original research gives brands something valuable in an increasingly crowded search landscape: information that isn’t available everywhere else.

That advantage may become even more important as AI search changes how people discover information. A recent Search Engine Land analysis of AI citations found that proprietary data can be a strong differentiator for brands seeking visibility in AI-generated answers.

The research highlights two factors that can work together when brands publish original information. The first is having something unique to contribute. The second is making that information easy to find.

Original Data Gives AI Systems Something Unique to Cite

AI systems have access to an enormous amount of information. When the same statistics, explanations, and observations appear across numerous websites, individual pages can have a difficult time standing out.

Proprietary data gives brands an opportunity to offer something different. This can take the shape of:

When an AI system needs to answer a question related to that subject, unique findings give it a source that offers information beyond the standard answers already circulating online.

The research also found that information appearing earlier on a page was more likely to receive an AI citation.

That finding gives marketers another factor to consider when organizing content. If an important statistic is buried several sections into an article, an AI system may have a harder time identifying it as one of the page’s key contributions.

When a piece of original research is central to a page, introducing the finding earlier can make the information easier for both AI systems and readers to locate.
